passage.title: The street that started talking
passage.subtitle: How a group chat turned 64 houses into a community – and what went wrong along the way

blocks.text: For the first eleven years he lived on Hawthorn Road, Desmond Clarke knew the names of exactly three of his neighbours. That changed on a freezing night in February two years ago, when a storm brought down power lines across the north of Leeds and left the street's 64 houses without electricity for almost two days. Clarke, a retired postman, did something he had never done before: he went from door to door with a torch and a notebook, asking whether anyone needed help and writing down phone numbers.

By the time the lights came back on, he had collected 41 numbers and set up a group chat called 'Hawthorn Helpers'. At first it was used only for practical things. A woman at number 12 who had a gas cooker offered to boil water for families with babies, and a student lent his camping heater to an elderly couple who had been sitting in their coats all day. 'I assumed it would go quiet once the emergency was over,' Clarke says. 'Instead, it just kept growing.'

Two years later, the group has 118 members – almost every household on the street, plus a few from neighbouring roads – and its messages paint a picture of everyday life. People lend each other ladders and drills, pass on children's clothes that no longer fit, and post photos of cats that have wandered into the wrong garden. A shared spreadsheet lists who is happy to take in parcels when a neighbour is out, and every October the street holds a 'swap and soup' afternoon, at which residents exchange things they no longer want and eat soup cooked by whoever owns the biggest pan.

Researchers who study local communities say that such groups can have surprisingly large effects. Dr Priya Nair, a sociologist in Manchester, has followed neighbourhood chats in five British cities. 'Most of what happens in them looks trivial,' she says. 'Someone has lost a glove, someone needs a lift to the station. But those small exchanges build trust, and trust is what people rely on when something serious happens.' In her research, people living on streets with an active group were twice as likely to say they would ask a neighbour for help in an emergency as people on similar streets without one.

The group has not always been a friendly place, however. Last spring, an argument about parking – a long-running source of tension on a street built a century before most families owned a car – became so bitter that several members left. On another occasion, a message warning about a 'suspicious man' walking slowly past the houses turned out to be about a new neighbour from Eritrea who was trying to work out which front door was his. 'That one made me feel ashamed,' says Clarke. 'He was welcomed with a cake the next day, but it showed how quickly these groups can turn people against each other.'

Since then, the chat has had a short list of rules, drawn up by a committee of five volunteers. Nobody may be described as suspicious unless a crime has actually been committed, political discussions are not allowed, and anyone who wants to complain about a neighbour is asked to knock on that neighbour's door first. Clarke admits that the rules are not always followed, but he believes they have made the group calmer.

For many members, though, the group's real value is not practical at all. Margaret Ellis, 84, who has lived on Hawthorn Road since 1962, says she now has someone to talk to almost every day. 'I hardly use the chat myself – my granddaughter had to show me how it works,' she says. 'But since it started, people stop me in the street. They know my name now.'

example.prompt: What did Desmond Clarke do for a living before he retired?
example.explanation: A postman (postás). A szöveg szerint Clarke nyugdíjas postás („a retired postman”), tehát nyugdíjba vonulása előtt postásként dolgozott.

items.prompt: For how long was Hawthorn Road without electricity after the storm?
items.explanation: Almost two days (majdnem két napig). A vihar leszakította a vezetékeket, és az utca 64 háza majdnem két napig áram nélkül maradt.
items.evidence: left the street's 64 houses without electricity for almost two days

items.prompt: What did the woman at number 12 offer to do for families with babies?
items.explanation: Boil water (vizet forralni). A 12-es számú házban lakó nőnek gáztűzhelye volt, így áramszünetben is fel tudott ajánlani, hogy vizet forral a kisbabás családoknak.
items.evidence: A woman at number 12 who had a gas cooker offered to boil water for families with babies

items.prompt: Which items that children have grown out of do neighbours pass on to each other?
items.explanation: Children's clothes (gyerekruhák). A „grown out of” (kinőtte) a szöveg „that no longer fit” (ami már nem jó rájuk) kifejezésének átfogalmazása: a szomszédok továbbadják egymásnak a kinőtt gyerekruhákat.
items.evidence: pass on children's clothes that no longer fit

items.prompt: According to Dr Nair, what do small everyday exchanges between neighbours build?
items.explanation: Trust (bizalom). Dr Nair szerint az apró, jelentéktelennek tűnő szívességek bizalmat építenek, és erre a bizalomra támaszkodnak az emberek, amikor valami komoly történik.
items.evidence: But those small exchanges build trust

items.prompt: How much more likely were people on streets with an active group to say they would ask a neighbour for help in an emergency?
items.explanation: Twice as likely (kétszer akkora eséllyel). A kutatás szerint az aktív csoporttal rendelkező utcák lakói kétszer olyan valószínűséggel mondták, hogy vészhelyzetben segítséget kérnének egy szomszédtól, mint a hasonló, csoport nélküli utcák lakói.
items.evidence: were twice as likely to say they would ask a neighbour for help in an emergency

items.prompt: What was the argument that made several members leave the group about?
items.explanation: Parking (parkolás). Tavaly tavasszal a parkolásról szóló vita – ami régóta feszültséget okoz egy olyan utcában, amely jóval az autók elterjedése előtt épült – annyira elmérgesedett, hogy többen kiléptek a csoportból.

items.prompt: Who was the 'suspicious man' described in the warning message?
items.explanation: A new neighbour (egy új szomszéd). A „gyanús férfi” valójában egy Eritreából érkezett új szomszéd volt, aki csak azt próbálta kitalálni, melyik bejárati ajtó az övé.
items.evidence: turned out to be about a new neighbour from Eritrea who was trying to work out which front door was his

items.prompt: What are members who want to complain about a neighbour asked to do first?
items.explanation: Knock on their door (kopogjanak be hozzá). A csoport szabályai szerint aki panaszkodni akar egy szomszédra, annak először be kell kopognia az illető ajtaján, vagyis személyesen beszélnie vele, mielőtt a csoportban panaszkodna.
items.evidence: anyone who wants to complain about a neighbour is asked to knock on that neighbour's door first

items.prompt: Who taught Margaret Ellis how to use the chat?
items.explanation: Her granddaughter (az unokája). Margaret elmondja, hogy alig használja a csoportot, és az unokájának kellett megmutatnia neki, hogyan működik („had to show me how it works”) – a kérdés „taught … how to use” kifejezése ezt fogalmazza át.
items.evidence: my granddaughter had to show me how it works
